Double Fine’s 99-player launch, Picardo blames politics for Starfleet Academy, Xbox’s AI post and more | The Reef Daily 
https://t.co/tqS7NvCTX4

Tim Schafer at the 2018 GDC IGF Awards. Photo: Official GDC, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 (cropped)

Double Fine’s new game, Thank You, Bus Driver, peaked at 99 players on Steam, and Kneon thinks the studio has bigger problems than its failed union drive. Also on the list: an Xbox manager who said everybody in games uses AI and then deleted his account, Robert Picardo’s newest reason Starfleet Academy got canceled and Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie going on ice. Further down, the Halo remakes that reportedly never happened, Modern Warfare 4’s early reviews and the newest Clownfish TV podcast episodes.

New Clownfish TV episodes

How many people are playing Double Fine’s Thank You, Bus Driver?

Almost nobody. The game peaked at 99 players at once on Steam, according to the report Kneon reads, and by the end of the recording only 16 people were playing. For comparison, he points out that Concord had about 700. Less than a day earlier came word that Day of the Tentacle Remastered and Full Throttle Remastered are leaving Game Pass. Double Fine’s games had stayed on the service since the studio joined Xbox in 2019.

Then Kotaku piled on. Its report says a majority of eligible Double Fine employees filed for a union with the National Labor Relations Board earlier this year and withdrew the petition two weeks later. When 23 people were laid off soon after, Kotaku reports, all eight organizers who signed it were among them. Tim Schafer told Kotaku that “in general, I’m pro-union.”

Kneon’s read is simpler. Any indie developer could put a game on Steam and beat 21 players, he says, and a studio in that spot has to make games people will pay for first.

Did an Xbox manager really say everyone uses AI?

Yes, and then he deleted his X account. An Xbox business strategy manager posted that Microsoft uses AI “just as all companies do in 2026” and that developers who won’t use it shouldn’t be in the business. He also wrote, “I’m happy to take the hit if it means hundreds can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” He deleted the account after the replies piled up, sources told PC Gamer.

Kneon agrees with him. Refusing AI now is like doing long division while everybody else uses a calculator, he says, and Microsoft spends too much on Copilot to keep it out of its games.

The episode also covers a report, built on anonymous sources, that more Xbox layoffs are planned for October, November and January. The same report puts Microsoft’s internal estimate for its next console, Project Helix, at $1,200 to $1,800 unless Microsoft subsidizes it. And some Xbox owners say Microsoft emailed them about trading their consoles in at Best Buy for up to $375.

Why does Robert Picardo say Starfleet Academy was canceled?

Politics, this time. Picardo said “the present political moment in our culture” made Star Trek’s core values “out of fashion temporarily.” Fandom Pulse counts that as his fourth explanation since Paramount+ announced on March 24 that the show would end after Season 2. The earlier ones blamed a lack of ads, Paramount’s new owners, Elon Musk and Stephen Miller.

Fandom Pulse also pulled the numbers. None of the first 10 episodes made Nielsen’s weekly streaming top 10, and by June the show had an 85% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes next to a 52% audience score.

Kneon has loved Star Trek: The Next Generation since he was about 10, and he says the show just wasn’t good. He calls it “a CW show in space.” Even Enterprise star Dominic Keating said on his own podcast, with Picardo sitting across from him, that it was “a bit CW in space.”

Is Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie canceled?

On ice, in his words. Waititi told Inverse, while promoting Klara and the Sun, “we’re going to actually put it on ice and we’re working on a different thing altogether.” Kneon guesses Rian Johnson’s long-promised Star Wars trilogy is dead too.

The hosts also get into artist Frank Cho’s claim, made in a podcast interview at New York Comic Con, that he has been banned from Marvel for three years. “I pissed off Kathleen Kennedy and she demanded Marvel ban me,” Cho said. He says it started with joke Star Wars sketch covers he drew as convention commissions, and that Kennedy ended the whole Star Wars sketch cover program over them. Bleeding Cool, which reported the interview, couldn’t find new Marvel work from Cho after 2022.

The hosts expect a lot more stories like this now that Kennedy is gone from Lucasfilm. Somebody, they figure, will write the tell-all.

every AI model you have ever used - GPT-4, claude, gemini, llama, grok - is doing one thing. one single mathematical operation underneath every answer, every line of code, every image, every agent action.

it is computing bayes' theorem. an equation written by a presbyterian minister in 1763 who never published it because he thought it was too obvious.

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B)

thomas bayes died in 1761. his friend richard price found the manuscript in a drawer and published it posthumously. neither of them could have imagined that 263 years later this equation would power a $4.6 trillion industry.

here's what the equation actually does inside your model -

every token a transformer generates is a bayesian update. the model starts with a prior - its training data, its weights, its compressed knowledge of the internet. then it conditions on your prompt. every word you type shifts the probability distribution. the output is the posterior - the most probable next token given everything the model knows plus everything you just said.

P(next token | your prompt) = P(your prompt | next token) × P(next token) / P(your prompt)

this is not an analogy. this is literally the softmax function. the attention mechanism is bayesian inference running in parallel across every token in the context window simultaneously.

now watch why this matters for the frontier labs -

the quality of any bayesian system depends on two things: the prior and the likelihood function. in LLM terms: the training data and the architecture.

openai's strategy since GPT-2: make the prior bigger. more data. more parameters. more compressed internet. this is why GPT-4 cost $100 million+ to train. they were building the most expensive prior in history.

the problem: bayes' theorem has a known failure mode. when the prior is trained on data that contains errors, the posterior inherits those errors and amplifies them. this is called prior contamination. every statistician learns it in their first year.

the measurement [Table 1] -

estimated error rate in GPT-4's training data: 3-5% of tokens contain factual errors, outdated information, or contradictions.
estimated hallucination rate of GPT-4: 3-8% depending on domain.

the correlation is not a coincidence. it is bayes' theorem doing exactly what bayes proved it would do. garbage prior, garbage posterior. 263 years ago.

anthropic understood this first. dario amodei's entire approach - constitutional AI, RLHF, careful data curation - is not a safety strategy. it is a bayesian strategy. reduce contamination in the prior. the posterior improves automatically.

this is why claude hallucinates less than GPT-4 on most benchmarks despite being a smaller model. it is not smarter. it has a cleaner prior.

google understood it second. gemini's mixture-of-experts architecture splits the prior into specialized domains. medical knowledge in one expert, legal in another, code in a third. each expert has a smaller, more focused prior with less contamination. bayes' theorem operates more accurately on a focused prior than a noisy universal one.

now watch the scaling paradox [Fig. 1] -

more training data should make models better. bayes says a larger prior is more informative.

but the internet is not growing cleaner. it is growing noisier. AI-generated content now accounts for an estimated 15-25% of new internet text. models training on AI-generated text are feeding bayesian priors built on bayesian posteriors.

this is recursive prior contamination. bayes proved exactly what happens:

generation 1: model trained on human data. error rate 3%.
generation 2: model trained on mix of human + AI data. error rate 5.4%.
generation 3: projected error rate 9.1%.
generation 4: projected error rate 16.7%.

the curve is exponential. each generation's errors compound into the next generation's prior. this is not a hypothetical - researchers at oxford and cambridge published the empirical measurements in july 2025. they called it "model collapse."

bayes called it contaminated priors. in 1763.

the companies that survive this are the ones with proprietary human-generated data that has never been touched by AI output. this is why reddit sold its data to google for $60 million. this is why twitter/X locked its API. this is why stack overflow mass-signed licensing deals. clean human data is the new oil. because it is the only thing that produces a clean bayesian prior.

the next breakthrough in AI will not come from a bigger model. it will come from a cleaner prior. the difference between those two strategies is the difference between openai spending $10 billion on GPT-5 and someone spending $500 million on the most carefully curated dataset ever assembled.

bayes proved it. a minister who thought his equation was too obvious to publish.

263 years later it governs every AI company on earth and almost none of them talk about it by name.

If you are AGI-pilled, a capability maximalist, an x-risk person, etc. this data has to move you at some point, right?

https://t.co/U5f3D9zMrQ

Slow diffusion can only be part of the story, esp. given such muted employment / productivity effects in coding as late as this spring (see: https://t.co/rkfmrqvRVn).

IMO everyone should be thinking more about the variety of structural limitations faced by LLMs, things like hallucination, reward-hacking, context rot, insufficient data esp. outside of math/SWE, poor generalization, unpredictability (same prompt, different outputs), user-sensitivity (output quality is a function of use quality), mode collapse (model outputs lack humanlike diversity), the uncodifiability of much of humans' load-bearing tacit knowledge, and cultural stigma/anti-inductive norms (AI outputs become cheap, low-status baselines).

One red flag for me in a lot of maximalist AI discourse is the assumption that models being (in some sense) intelligent, and their becoming more intelligent, licenses any and all inferences about what they might do. This is similar to the oft-made "intelligence-as-magic" objection.

The problem here is that there are many different kinds of intelligence, with unique powers and limitations, and the wider world can relate to each one in different ways. I have yet to encounter a serious attempt to characterize the unique KIND of intelligence LLMs have.

The more I think about it, the more I think that the term "artificial intelligence" may be part of the problem here, and that it would actually be less misleading in certain respects to construe LLMs as "artificial organisms" or "lifeforms."

This has its own risks of course, but if nothing else it cuts against the impression that LLMs are ethereal demigods on the road to full omniscience, and suggests instead that they are more like animals with a set of capacities we can come to constrain and understand. It could also help us better explore their strange variety of distributed silicon embodiment, and the related fact that they need to consume scarce resources to survive.

This picture seems closer to the truth to me.

The caption isn't wrong, but you’ve misinterpreted the text.

The text in the image is not claiming that they are the same company; rather, it is a summary highlighting a strategic partnership they entered into and outlining what they have in common as separate financial entities.

Moody's (Moody's Corporation) primarily famous as one of the Big Three credit rating agencies, evaluating the creditworthiness of debt securities.

MSCI (Morgan Stanley Capital International) is an independent provider of global equity indexes, portfolio risk analysis, and ESG ratings.

The July 2024 partnership: the text mentions a specific event in July 2024, Moody's and MSCI formed a strategic agreement to leverage each other's data.

- MSCI's role: agreed to integrate Moody’s sustainability ratings and data into its models.

- Moody's role: agreed to use MSCI’s industry-leading ESG research and ratings content across its financial platforms.

What they have in mommon?

As the second heading in your image suggests, they share a market sector. Both companies operate as global financial data and analytics leaders, serving the same institutional clients (like investment banks and asset managers) even though their core products (credit ratings vs stock indexes) are different.
